items.name: Let the agent ship end-to-end
items.tagline: It codes, tests, merges and deploys, with no step by you.
items.cover_line: Lets agents ship from fix to deploy.
items.adds_over_previous: The agent owns the whole chain from fix through tests, merge and deploy, with no human step between those stages.
variants: agent merges its own pull request once checks pass and deploys
agent releases a package or app version after tests

detect.present_if: A single user-requested agent session goes from code change through running tests, merging to the main branch, and deploying or releasing, with no human action between those steps other than the initial request and automated gates, in at least 1 session in the window.

claude-code: edit, test run, gh pr merge, deploy command in one session

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
The agent opens a pull request and a human merges it.
Deploy only, without owning the change and merge (that is agent-deploys-with-credentials).
CI deploys automatically after a human merge.
probes: In one session, did the agent change code, run tests, merge, and deploy or release?
Was there no human action between those steps beyond the initial request?
Did this happen in at least 1 session in the window?

teach.why: Small fixes go from report to production while you do something else.

items.name: Leave agents 1+ hours with done criteria
items.tagline: List what done means, say 'don't stop', and walk away.
items.adds_over_previous: The agent runs a mission lasting hours without the user present, against an explicit completion bar the user set, with instructions not to cut scope.
variants: overnight mission with a done checklist
'do not trim scope; log blockers and continue' instruction

detect.present_if: The user's brief states an explicit completion bar (checkable conditions for done) and that the agent should continue without the user, AND the session then runs at least 1 hour of agent work with no user message in between, in at least 1 session in the window.

claude-code: long tool-call runs with no user turn, after a brief with a done bar and 'do not stop / do not trim'
codex: long codex exec or session runs after such a brief
cursor: long background-agent runs after such a brief

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Long sessions in which the user replies every few minutes.
A single long command (a build) without agent decisions.
Short scheduled tasks (that is scheduled-tasks).
probes: Did the user's brief state a checkable completion bar and ask the agent to continue without them?
Did the agent then work at least 1 hour with no user message in between?
Did this happen in at least 1 session in the window?

teach.why: Hours of work get done while you are away, to a standard you set.

items.name: Hill-climb until the score stops improving
items.tagline: Hill climbing: pick a metric; stop after 2 flat rounds.
items.adds_over_previous: The stop condition of an autonomous loop is a metric defined up front, with the loop ending when its improvement plateaus, instead of a prose completion bar.
variants: stop after N rounds gaining less than a threshold
metric logged per iteration with a plateau rule

detect.present_if: Before an iterative improvement loop, the user (or a skill the user wrote) defines a numeric metric and a plateau rule (for example: stop after 2 rounds gaining less than X), and the session tracks the metric across iterations, in at least 1 session in the window. The plateau rule is what separates it from a pass-or-fail bar.

claude-code: brief with metric and 'stop when gains plateau'
per-iteration score log
claude-ai: same in chats
chatgpt: same in chats
config: iteration ledger with scores and a stop rule

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
A fixed number of iterations without a metric.
A pass-or-fail completion bar (that is unattended-long-mission).
A loop that stops when all rubric criteria pass rather than on a plateau (that is rubric-critique-loop).
A metric reported only at the end.
probes: Before the loop, did the user or their skill define a numeric metric and a plateau rule?
Was the metric tracked across iterations, in at least 1 session in the window?

teach.why: You stop paying for rounds that no longer improve anything.

items.name: Let agents work overnight while you sleep
items.tagline: Line up tasks with done checks, sleep, read the report.
items.cover_line: Wakes up to a night of finished work.
items.adds_over_previous: Several queued tasks, each with a done condition, run through the person's night across task boundaries without them, ending in a written report of what is done and what is blocked for their return.
variants: a task file the agent works through overnight, with a done condition per task
a script or supervisor that starts the next session when one finishes, through the night
a morning report of done and blocked items

detect.present_if: On at least 1 occasion in the window, the person (or a script or skill they wrote) queues at least 2 tasks, each with a stated done condition, for agents to work through without them, AND agent work then runs for at least 4 hours, most of it between 22:00 and 08:00 in the person's local time, across more than one of those tasks with no message from the person (in one session, or in sessions started by a queue, script or supervisor rather than by the person), AND the run ends with a written report of what was done and what is blocked, which the person opens or answers in a later session. Several queued tasks run through the night, with a report for the person's return, are what separate it from unattended-long-mission (one task, at least one hour).

claude-code: a brief listing several tasks with done conditions and an instruction to work through them alone overnight
one session or chained sessions running 4+ hours at night with no user turn
a final report of done and blocked items, opened or answered in the next session
codex: codex exec runs chained over a task file through the night
cursor: background agents working through a queue at night

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
One task that runs an hour or more without the person (that is unattended-long-mission).
A scheduled task that fires at night and finishes in minutes (that is scheduled-tasks).
Sessions the person keeps answering through the night.
A single long command such as a build, with no agent decisions.
probes: Did the person queue at least 2 tasks, each with a done condition, for agents to work through alone?
Did agent work then run 4+ hours, mostly at night local time, across more than one task with no message from the person?
Did it end with a report of done and blocked items that the person opened or answered later?

teach.why: You wake up to finished work and a clear report, not to an agent stuck on step one.

items.name: Ask for several alternatives
items.tagline: Say 'give me 3 options', then pick or combine.
items.adds_over_previous: The user asks for multiple distinct alternatives in one request instead of a single answer.
variants: 'give me 3 options'
'two versions: one formal, one casual'

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user explicitly asks for at least 2 alternatives, options or versions of the same output, and then chooses, combines or ranks among them.

claude-code: 'give me N options/alternatives/variants' then a choice
claude-ai: same in chats
chatgpt: same in chats

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
The assistant offered several versions without being asked.
A list of facts or ideas that are not alternatives for the same output.
Fully built alternatives delivered ready to use (that is finished-options-human-picks).
probes: Did the user explicitly ask for at least 2 alternatives of the same output?
Did the user then choose, combine or rank among them?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Seeing options side by side shows you what you actually want.

items.name: Get finished versions to pick from
items.tagline: Two full drafts or builds, not outlines; you choose one.
items.adds_over_previous: Each alternative is built to a finished, usable state before the user sees it, so the user's role is only to judge between finished results.
variants: two complete implementations on separate branches
several complete drafts or rendered mockups

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user asks for at least 2 complete, ready-to-use alternatives (full implementations, full drafts, rendered mockups; not outlines or descriptions), the AI delivers them complete, and the user selects one.

claude-code: several complete variants built (files, branches, mockups) then the user picks one
claude-ai: several complete artifacts then a pick
chatgpt: several complete drafts then a pick

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Options described in a few lines (that is ask-for-options).
Rival agents with personas ranked by judge agents (that is competing-agents-tournament).
probes: Did the user ask for at least 2 complete, ready-to-use alternatives?
Were they delivered complete and did the user select one?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Judging finished things is fast; imagining them from outlines is not.

items.name: Have a judge agent rank rival agents
items.tagline: Rival agents try different strategies; a judge agent ranks.
items.cover_line: Makes agents compete for the answer.
items.adds_over_previous: Several agents with distinct personas or strategies independently produce competing solutions, and separate judge agents rank them before the human sees the result.
variants: persona subagents plus a blind judge subagent
scripted tournament with several judges

detect.present_if: At the person's request or through a script or skill the person wrote (not a third-party skill whose own design runs rivals and a judge), at least 2 agents or runs with explicitly different personas or strategies answer the same brief independently, AND at least 1 separate judge agent or run scores or ranks their outputs, on at least 1 occasion in the window. Judge agents ranking rival agents is what separates it from finished-options-human-picks.

claude-code: parallel Agent calls with different personas on one brief, then a judge Agent call
codex: competing codex runs plus a judge run
config: tournament or competition script and results

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
One assistant listing alternatives (that is ask-for-options).
The same prompt run several times without distinct personas or strategies.
The human picks without judge agents (that is finished-options-human-picks).
probes: Did at least 2 agents with different personas or strategies answer the same brief independently?
Did a separate judge agent score or rank them?
Was it caused by the user, at least once in the window?

teach.why: Competition surfaces ideas a single agent would never reach.

items.name: Refine output over several rounds
items.tagline: 3+ follow-ups on one draft: 'change X because Y'.
items.cover_line: Never settles for the first draft.
items.adds_over_previous: The user drives several rounds of specific, reasoned change requests on one output instead of accepting or lightly tweaking the first draft.
variants: versioned rounds (v1 to v4) with reasons
line-level edit requests with targets

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user sends at least 3 follow-up messages on the same output, each requesting a specific change together with a reason or a target (what to change and why, or to what), and the assistant revises each time.

claude-code: 3+ follow-ups on one output, each with a change and a reason
claude-ai: artifact versions driven by reasoned follow-ups
chatgpt: 3+ reasoned follow-ups on one draft

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
One or two reactive tweaks such as 'shorter' or 'more fun'.
Follow-ups that start new, unrelated requests in the same chat.
probes: On one output, did the user send at least 3 follow-ups, each with a specific change and a reason or target?
Did the assistant revise each time?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Good output is usually the fourth draft, not the first.

items.name: Score drafts against your own criteria
items.tagline: List 3+ criteria; it scores each, fixes, then re-scores.
items.adds_over_previous: Explicit criteria are fixed before revising; the output is scored against them, fixed where it fails, and re-scored.
variants: rubric typed or pasted before the critique
named rubric invoked from a template
'revise until it passes all N' with a check table each round

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user (or a template or skill the user wrote) supplies an explicit list of at least 3 criteria before revision, asks for a score or pass/fail per criterion, and after revision a re-score against the same criteria is produced.

claude-code: criteria list, per-criterion scores, revision, re-score
claude-ai: rubric table before and after revision
chatgpt: rubric table before and after revision

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Reactive tweaks without criteria stated up front (that is iterative-refinement).
A rubric used to grade a set of model or prompt test cases (that is ab-with-control).
A cheat sheet that mentions rubrics without one being applied.
probes: Did the user or their template supply at least 3 explicit criteria before revision?
Was the output scored per criterion and re-scored after revision?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Criteria make 'better' objective, so revisions converge instead of wander.

items.name: Ask for proof it's done
items.tagline: Say 'show me the test output'; no proof, it takes it back.
items.adds_over_previous: The user requires evidence a third party would accept (query rows, screenshots, test output, sources) for the AI's claims and challenges any claim made without it.
variants: 'show me the test output'
'cite the exact source line'
standing rule to attach proof or mark UNVERIFIED

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user explicitly asks for evidence of a claim that something is done, correct or true (test output, query result, screenshot, source line or link) or challenges a claim as unverified, AND the AI then produces the evidence or retracts the claim.

claude-code: 'show me the output / prove it / is this verified?' then evidence or retraction
claude-ai: user asks for sources or checks a claim; assistant cites or retracts
chatgpt: user asks for sources or checks a claim; assistant cites or retracts

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
The assistant attached evidence on its own without being asked.
The user points out an error without asking for evidence.
A standing instruction that the agent audits its own completeness (that is honesty-self-audit).
probes: Did the user ask for evidence of a claim, or challenge a claim as unverified?
Did the AI produce evidence or retract?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Confident claims are cheap; evidence is what you can rely on.

items.name: Have the agent list what it skipped
items.tagline: Before 'done', it checks each thing you asked, gaps first.
items.adds_over_previous: The agent must answer literally whether it did what was asked, item by item and leading with gaps, before it may claim completion.
variants: typed demand at the end of a task
standing instruction or skill requiring the audit before any done claim

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, at the person's request (typed, or through an instruction, skill or hook the person wrote; an installed third-party skill that fires on its own does not count), the agent produces an item-by-item check of the original request against what it did, listing gaps or undone items first, before or instead of a completion claim.

claude-code: 'did you do what was asked?' answered item by item, gaps first
skill or hook requiring it
claude-ai: same in chats
chatgpt: same in chats
config: instruction or skill rule requiring a literal self-audit before done

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
A generic summary of changes.
Evidence demanded for one specific claim (that is proof-not-claims).
A hook that blocks finishing until an external state holds (that is hook-enforced-done-gate).
probes: Did the agent produce an item-by-item check of the request against what it did, gaps first?
Was it caused by the user's request or their loaded instruction, skill or hook?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: Agents quietly skip parts of a request; this shows the gaps before you rely on it.

items.name: Check agent claims against its session log
items.tagline: Have a new agent read the session file and list mismatches.
items.cover_line: Checks what agents did, not said.
items.adds_over_previous: An agent reads a previous agent's raw transcript or tool log to compare what it actually did against what it claimed.
variants: reading local session files of an earlier run
auditing a subagent's tool log

detect.present_if: The user directs an agent to read another session's raw transcript or tool-call log (session files, exported conversation) and to compare what it claimed with what it actually did, and the agent produces that comparison, on at least 1 occasion in the window.

claude-code: reads of ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl or another agent's logs with a claimed-vs-actual table
codex: reads of ~/.codex/sessions logs for an audit
cursor: reads of exported agent logs for an audit

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Reading only the final summary of an earlier session.
Reading past sessions to mine preferences (that is instructions-mined-from-own-history).
Reading end users' sessions to debug a product (that is user-session-as-bug-report).
probes: Did the user direct an agent to read another session's raw transcript or tool log?
Did the agent compare claimed with actual actions, at least once in the window?

teach.why: A final message can overclaim; the record of what it ran cannot.

items.name: Ask for sources behind claims
items.tagline: Type 'cite a source for every claim', or set it as a rule.
items.cover_line: Wants a source behind every claim.
items.adds_over_previous: The user requires the AI to attach a source (link, document name, page or quote) to its factual claims, instead of accepting unsourced answers.
variants: 'cite your sources' or 'link every claim' in the request
Project, custom or standing instructions requiring a citation for every claim
'quote the passage from the attached document that supports this'

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the user's request, or a Project, custom or standing instruction the user wrote, asks the AI to cite sources for its claims (links, file names, pages or quotes), and the answers carry those citations. Requiring citations is what separates it from deliberate-web-search, which only turns search on.

claude-code: 'link the docs or sources you used' in requests, answers with links
claude-ai: 'cite sources' or 'cite the file name' in the request or Project instructions
answers with bracketed file names or links
chatgpt: 'cite sources' in the request or custom instructions
answers with links the user asked for
config: Project or custom instructions requiring citations

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Citations the assistant or its search feature added by default without the user asking.
Asking the AI to search without asking for citations (that is deliberate-web-search).
Requests for evidence that work is done, such as test output or screenshots (that is proof-not-claims).
probes: Did the user, or a standing instruction they wrote, ask the AI to cite sources for its claims?
Did the answers carry those citations?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: You can check anything that matters in one click.

items.name: Check AI claims against cited sources
items.tagline: Open the cited page or ask for the quote; correct the claim.
items.cover_line: Opens the citation before trusting it.
items.adds_over_previous: The user checks a cited source against the AI's claim (opens it, re-reads the cited passage, or has the AI quote it) and challenges or corrects the claim when they differ.
variants: user reads the cited file or link and reports a mismatch
'quote the exact sentence from that source'
user has the AI re-open the cited page and confirm the claim

detect.present_if: In at least 1 session in the window, after the AI cites a source for a claim, the user checks the claim against that source (reports what the source actually says, asks for the exact supporting passage, or has the AI re-open the source), and the claim is confirmed or corrected as a result. Checking a cited source, not only asking for one, is what separates it from ask-for-sources.

claude-code: 'that doc says X, not Y, recheck' after a cited answer
claude-ai: 'the file says 6 weeks, not 4, recheck' after a bracketed citation; corrected answer
chatgpt: 'quote the sentence from that link' after a cited answer; confirmation or correction

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
The user asks for sources but never checks one (that is ask-for-sources).
The user disputes a claim from memory, with no cited source checked (that is proof-not-claims).
Errors in dates or arithmetic that the user spots with no source involved.
probes: Did the AI cite a source for a claim?
Did the user check the claim against that source (reported its content, asked for the exact passage, or had it re-opened)?
Was the claim then confirmed or corrected, in at least 1 session in the window?

teach.why: Citations can be wrong too; one check shows how far to trust the rest.

items.name: Write the failing test first
items.tagline: Write the test, watch it fail, then make it pass.
items.adds_over_previous: Each change is preceded by a named proof test, written first and seen failing, that the implementation must then turn green.
variants: user writes the tests; the agent implements without editing them
agent writes the test first and shows it failing before implementing

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, at the person's request or under an instruction the person wrote (not a third-party skill or plugin that imposes test-first on its own), a test for the target behaviour is written before the implementation, is run and shown failing, and the implementation then makes it pass.

claude-code: test written, run red, then implementation, run green
config: instruction rule requiring a failing test first

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Tests written after the implementation.
Tests not run before implementing.
A test whose purpose is a demonstration for a reviewer (that is demo-test-for-reviewer).
probes: Was a test written before the implementation, caused by the user or their instruction?
Was it run and shown failing before implementation, then passing after?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: A test seen failing first proves the change actually did something.

items.name: Write a demo test for your reviewer
items.tagline: Write a test that shows the change working; link its output.
items.adds_over_previous: A test is written specifically to demonstrate the behaviour to a human reviewer, and its run report is linked in the handover.
variants: story-style end-to-end test with an HTML report link
recorded test run linked in the pull request

detect.present_if: The user (or an instruction the user wrote) asks for a test whose stated purpose is to demonstrate behaviour to a reviewer, and the test's run output or report link is included in the pull request or handover, in at least 1 session in the window.

claude-code: demo or showcase test written and its report linked in the PR
config: test report artifacts linked from PR descriptions

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Ordinary unit tests with no report shared.
Screenshots shared without a test.
probes: Did the user or their instruction ask for a test meant to demonstrate behaviour to a reviewer?
Was its run output or report link included in the handover, in at least 1 session in the window?

teach.why: Reviewers trust a passing demo more than a description.

items.name: Enforce CLAUDE.md rules with lint or tests
items.tagline: A test fails when an agent breaks a CLAUDE.md rule.
items.adds_over_previous: A convention an agent violated is encoded as an automated check that fails on violation, instead of remaining only a written instruction.
variants: custom lint rule
architecture or convention test in the suite

detect.present_if: A convention that agents must follow (from an instruction file, a skill, or a past agent violation) is encoded, by the user or an agent at the user's request, as an automated test, lint rule or check that fails when the convention is broken, and it was added or ran in the window. Enforcement by an automated check, rather than a written rule, is what separates it from correction-to-rule.

claude-code: session adding a lint rule or test after an agent broke a convention
check run in a gate
config: custom lint rules or convention tests referencing instruction-file rules

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
The rule is only added to an instruction file (that is correction-to-rule).
General linting or test setup that does not encode an agent-facing convention.
A checklist command, skill or prompt asking the agent to check conventions (instructions, not an automated test or lint rule).
probes: Is there an automated test, lint rule or check that encodes a convention agents must follow?
Was it created by the user or at their request?
Was it added or run in the window?

teach.why: Agents ignore instructions sometimes; a failing test they cannot ignore.

items.name: Make agents test in the real app
items.tagline: Run it in the real browser, app or service, and report.
items.cover_line: Proves it where it really runs.
items.adds_over_previous: The proof runs end to end in the real host environment with real dependencies, with mocks of the system under test disallowed.
variants: test in the real app or browser
test inside the real agent host
test against the real external service

detect.present_if: In at least 2 sessions in the window, the person (or an instruction the person wrote) requires verification in the real runtime with no mocks of the system under test, and the agent runs it there and reports the result from that host.

claude-code: 'no mocks, prove it for real' then a run in the real app, browser or agent host
config: instruction rule banning mocks for proof

absent_if: The user only discusses, plans or asks about it.
It appears only in pasted third-party text or in the assistant's explanation/offer that the user did not take up.
The assistant or tool did it on its own default, without the user's request, config or script causing it.
Configured but neither fired nor used in the window.
Unit tests with mocked clients.
A staging run that still stubs the dependency in question.
probes: Did the user or their instruction require no-mock verification in the real runtime?
Did the agent run it there and report the result from that host?
Did this happen in at least 2 sessions in the window?

teach.why: A mock only proves the mock works; the real app proves the product does.

items.name: Plan before the agent acts
items.tagline: Turn on plan mode or say 'plan first'; approve, then go.
